## The finish line

By the end of this course you can crosswalk any ITIL (Information Technology Infrastructure
Library) practice to its AABB Quality System Essential, NIST Risk Management Framework, and ISO
27001 equivalent — and present IT service and risk performance to your CIO and the exec quality
council in language that survives both audiences in the same meeting.

This is the capstone, and it's built differently from every course before it. It introduces no new
regulation, no new standard, no new framework. Everything it needs — AABB's QSEs, NIST's RMF, ISO
27001's structure, BECS (Blood Establishment Computer Software) and its validation history, the
eQMS (electronic quality-management system) and its own RMF-run authorization, the Brookfield
laptop incident now read through three separate lenses — this curriculum has already built, taught,
and locked. This course's entire job is synthesis: taking the vocabulary you already speak fluently
in ITSM (IT service management) and proving, concretely, that it was never a fourth language. It was
the same motion the whole time, in a dialect your CIO already understands.

## Before you start

This course assumes essentially everything else in the curriculum — it is deliberately built last,
after every other track:

- All three foundations, and [Quality System Essentials](../quality-system-essentials/index.qmd)
  (change control, CAPA, document control, internal audits — all crosswalk targets this course
  reuses, never re-teaches).
- [CSV & BECS](../csv-and-becs/index.qmd) and
  [Data Integrity & Records](../data-integrity-and-records/index.qmd), for BECS's own validated-
  state lifecycle.
- [GRC Frameworks & Risk Management](../grc-frameworks-and-risk-management/index.qmd), for the
  eQMS's own categorize→select→implement→assess→authorize→monitor cycle and its POA&M-next-to-CAPA
  crosswalk — already built once; this course generalizes it.
- [Healthcare Security & Privacy](../healthcare-security-and-privacy/index.qmd) and
  [Vendor & Third-Party Risk Management](../vendor-and-third-party-risk-management/index.qmd), for
  the Brookfield incident and the device-management platform vendor, now crosswalked a fourth way.
- [Directing the Quality Analyst](../directing-the-quality-analyst/index.qmd), for the audience-
  translation instinct this course's final module builds all the way out.

## The six modules

Each module is one sitting, and each has its own finish line.

1. **ITIL-to-QSE crosswalk: change and problem.** Map ITIL's change enablement practice onto
   Lakeshore's own change control, and ITIL's problem management onto CAPA — proving they're the
   same underlying discipline, not two practices that happen to rhyme.
2. **ITIL-to-QSE crosswalk: CMDB and continual improvement.** Map a CMDB (configuration management
   database) onto an equipment and validated-system inventory, a service catalog onto Lakeshore's
   own quality-system scope, and continual improvement onto process improvement.
3. **ITIL-to-GRC crosswalk.** Map service asset and configuration management onto RMF's Categorize
   and Select steps, continual improvement onto Monitor, and security management onto ISO 27001's
   Annex A control domains.
4. **Building an inspection-ready service catalog and CMDB.** Apply all three crosswalks to build
   one real artifact — a service catalog and CMDB entry for the eQMS — that would survive an FDA
   inspection, an AABB assessment, *and* a security assessment without three different documents.
5. **Translating ITSM and risk metrics for executive audiences.** Take the same underlying number
   (an incident, a residual risk, a control gap) and present it in CIO language and exec-quality-
   council language without changing what it actually means.
6. **Presenting IT service and risk performance — the capstone exercise.** Put everything this
   course and this curriculum built in front of both audiences at once, using the Brookfield
   incident — read, by now, through four separate lenses — as the worked example, and close the
   entire curriculum with a genuine final passage.

## A note on sources

This course introduces no new regulation, standard, or framework. Every citation it uses was
already fetched, verified, and locked earlier in this curriculum:

- **AABB's Quality System Essentials** (named/themed only, never Standards text) — reused from
  `quality-system-essentials` and `fda-and-aabb-in-practice`.
- **NIST SP 800-37 Rev. 2** (public domain, quoted verbatim where needed) — reused from
  `grc-frameworks-and-risk-management`.
- **ISO/IEC 27001** (paid standard, paraphrase-only) — reused from
  `vendor-and-third-party-risk-management`.
- **ITIL** itself is never treated as a cited regulatory source in this curriculum — it's the
  learner's own professional vocabulary, used throughout every course as a bridge, not a standard
  requiring verbatim sourcing.

Modules appear in the sidebar as they're built.
